name: Cloud Platforms
description: AWS, Azure and GCP core services, the shared responsibility model, IAM, networking and cost control.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Cloud Platforms is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is cloud computing?
cards.answer: Renting computing resources — servers, storage, databases, networking, AI services — on demand over the internet from a provider, paying for what you use instead of buying and running your own hardware.
cards.explanation: The cloud lets a team get a server in seconds and scale to thousands when traffic spikes. The trade-offs are ongoing costs that need watching and dependence on the provider.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-145 — The NIST definition of cloud computing

cards.prompt: Who are the big three cloud providers?
cards.answer: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). AWS is the largest; Azure is strong with Microsoft-centric enterprises; GCP is known for data and AI services.
cards.explanation: The core building blocks map closely across providers — virtual machines (EC2 / Azure VMs / Compute Engine), object storage (S3 / Blob Storage / Cloud Storage) — so concepts transfer even when names differ.

cards.prompt: What are IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
cards.answer: Infrastructure as a Service: rent raw virtual machines, storage and networks and manage everything above them (EC2). Platform as a Service: deploy your code and the provider runs the servers (Heroku, App Engine). Software as a Service: use finished software over the web (Gmail, Salesforce).
cards.explanation: Moving from IaaS to SaaS, you control less and manage less. Serverless functions (AWS Lambda) push PaaS further: you supply only a function and pay per invocation.

resources.title: Microsoft Azure — What is IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?

cards.prompt: What are regions and availability zones?
cards.answer: A region is a geographic area (e.g. eu-west-1, Ireland) containing several availability zones — separate data centres with independent power and networking. Spreading an application across zones survives a single data-centre failure.
cards.explanation: Choose regions close to users for speed and in the right jurisdiction for data-protection rules. Multi-region designs survive a whole region failing, at significant extra cost and complexity.

cards.prompt: What is the shared responsibility model?
cards.answer: The split of security duties between the cloud provider and the customer: the provider secures the cloud itself (data centres, hardware, the virtualisation layer); the customer secures what they put in it (their data, access permissions, configurations, code).
cards.explanation: Most cloud breaches are customer-side misconfigurations — a public storage bucket, an over-powerful access key — not failures of the provider.

modules.name: Core Concepts & Services
modules.description: The service categories every provider offers, and what the equivalents are called.

cards.prompt: Map the core services across AWS, Azure and GCP.
cards.answer: Compute: EC2 / Virtual Machines / Compute Engine. Objects: S3 / Blob Storage / Cloud Storage. Functions: Lambda / Azure Functions / Cloud Run functions. Managed Kubernetes: EKS / AKS / GKE. Managed SQL: RDS / Azure SQL Database / Cloud SQL. Identity: IAM / Entra ID / Cloud IAM.

right.title: Azure / GCP
points: AKS / GKE — GKE is the most mature Kubernetes
Azure: enterprise and AD integration; GCP: data and ML

cards.explanation: The primitives are the same everywhere; the differences are in defaults, quotas, IAM models and pricing. Knowing the shape of one provider transfers directly — learn concepts, then look up names.

resources.title: Google Cloud — AWS to GCP service comparison

cards.prompt: What is the shared responsibility model?
cards.answer: The provider secures the cloud — hardware, hypervisor, managed service internals. You secure what you put *in* it: your data, identities, access policies, network rules, OS patching on IaaS, and application code.
cards.explanation: Nearly every headline 'cloud breach' is a customer-side misconfiguration: a public bucket, an over-permissive role, an exposed database. The line moves with the service model — serverless shifts more to the provider, EC2 leaves patching to you.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between a region and an availability zone, and how should that shape a deployment?
cards.answer: A region is a geographic area; an availability zone is an isolated datacentre (or cluster) within it, with independent power, cooling and network. Deploy across at least two AZs for high availability; go multi-region only for disaster recovery or latency.
cards.explanation: Multi-AZ is nearly free and handles the common failure. Multi-region is expensive and hard — data replication, consistency, failover testing — so justify it with an actual RPO/RTO requirement rather than a vague wish for resilience.

cards.prompt: VMs vs containers vs serverless
cards.answer: VMs give full control and full operational burden; containers standardise packaging with orchestration overhead; serverless removes servers entirely at the cost of runtime constraints.

right.title: Serverless
points: Scales to zero and to thousands
Pay per request; excellent for spiky load

cards.explanation: Cost crosses over: serverless is far cheaper for bursty or low-volume workloads and more expensive at sustained high throughput. Migration difficulty differs too — a container runs anywhere, a function is written against one provider's event contract.

modules.name: IAM, Networking & Cost
modules.description: The three things that cause the most cloud incidents and invoices.

cards.prompt: A service needs to read one S3 bucket. What does the policy look like, and what mistake do people make?
cards.answer: A role with `s3:GetObject` scoped to `arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*`, assumed by the service — no long-lived keys. The common mistake is attaching a broad managed policy such as `AmazonS3FullAccess`, or worse, `*:*`.
cards.explanation: Use roles and instance/workload identity so credentials rotate automatically. Then let access analysers and 'last accessed' data prune what is unused. Start from the narrowest policy that works, not from the broadest one that stops the ticket.

cards.prompt: What are the pieces of a basic VPC design?
cards.answer: A CIDR block split into public and private subnets across AZs, an internet gateway for public egress and ingress, a NAT gateway for private egress, route tables per subnet, plus security groups (stateful, instance-level) and NACLs (stateless, subnet-level).
cards.explanation: Rule of thumb: only load balancers and bastions go in public subnets; applications and databases stay private. Security groups are the primary control — NACLs are a blunt secondary. VPC endpoints keep traffic to managed services off the public internet and cut NAT costs.

cards.prompt: Your cloud bill doubled with no traffic change. Where do you look?
cards.answer: Data egress (cross-AZ and internet), NAT gateway processing, idle or oversized instances, unattached volumes and old snapshots, log retention, and anything left running from a test. Tag everything and enable cost anomaly alerts.
cards.explanation: Egress and NAT are the classic silent costs — chatty cross-AZ services can cost more than the compute running them. The controls that work: budgets with alerts, autoscaling with sane minimums, storage lifecycle policies, and committed-use discounts for genuine baseline load.

cards.prompt: Managed database or run it yourself on VMs?
cards.answer: Managed, unless you have a specific need it cannot meet. You are paying for backups, patching, failover, monitoring and replication — all of which are expensive and easy to get subtly wrong.
cards.explanation: Self-hosting makes sense for unusual extensions, cost at very large scale, or hard portability requirements. Be honest about the operational cost: a database is a full-time responsibility, and 'we saved money' evaporates the first time a restore is needed and untested.

cards.prompt: What are the pillars of the Well-Architected Framework?
cards.answer: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation, and sustainability.
cards.explanation: It is useful mostly as a review checklist: walk each pillar against a design and the gaps show up quickly. The pillars trade against each other, so the point is making the trade explicit rather than pretending you can maximise all six.

modules.name: Core Services in Depth
modules.description: Object storage, messaging services, autoscaling, workload identity, account structure and pricing models.

cards.prompt: What are the key properties of object storage such as S3, and how is it different from a filesystem?
cards.answer: A flat namespace of buckets and keys holding immutable objects written and read whole over HTTP, with effectively unlimited capacity, eleven nines of durability and strong read-after-write consistency. There are no real directories, no appends and no in-place edits — you replace objects.
cards.explanation: Storage classes (standard, infrequent access, archive) plus lifecycle rules cut costs for ageing data. Block public access by default, enable versioning or object lock for important data, and use presigned URLs to let clients upload or download directly without proxying through your servers.

resources.title: AWS — S3 user guide — What is Amazon S3?

cards.prompt: Queue (SQS) vs pub/sub topic (SNS) vs event bus (EventBridge)
cards.answer: A queue delivers each message to one consumer for work distribution; a topic fans each message out to every subscriber; an event bus routes events to targets by matching rules on their content.
cards.explanation: Common composition: publish to a topic or bus, subscribe one queue per consuming service so each has its own buffer, retries and dead-letter queue. Standard queues give at-least-once, unordered delivery — design idempotent consumers; FIFO variants trade throughput for ordering per group.

resources.title: AWS — Messaging — choosing SQS, SNS or EventBridge

cards.prompt: Your service autoscales on CPU, but during traffic spikes latency degrades for minutes before new capacity helps. What do you change?
cards.answer: Scale on a signal closer to the demand (requests per target, queue depth, concurrency) rather than CPU, keep a warm minimum with headroom, shorten instance start time (smaller images, pre-warmed or pre-baked instances), and add scheduled or predictive scaling for known peaks.
cards.explanation: Reactive scaling always lags: metrics must breach, the policy must fire, and instances must boot and pass health checks. Set scale-in more conservatively than scale-out to avoid flapping, and cap the maximum so a bug or attack cannot scale your bill without bound.

resources.title: AWS — EC2 Auto Scaling — Target tracking scaling policies

cards.prompt: How should workloads authenticate to cloud APIs without long-lived access keys?
cards.answer: Through platform identity: instance profiles or IAM roles for compute, workload identity for Kubernetes service accounts, and OIDC federation for external systems such as CI — each exchanging a platform-issued token for short-lived, automatically rotated credentials.
cards.explanation: Long-lived keys leak through repositories, laptops and logs and are rarely rotated. With federation there is nothing static to steal, and trust policies can restrict which repository, branch or namespace may assume a role.

cards.prompt: Why do organisations split cloud usage into many accounts (or subscriptions/projects)?
cards.answer: Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary: separate accounts per environment and per workload limit the blast radius of a compromise or mistake, give clean cost attribution, and let organisation-level guardrails (service control policies, Azure Policy) apply per group.
cards.explanation: A landing zone sets this up consistently: centralised identity and SSO, logging to a locked-down security account, network hubs, and baseline guardrails. Retrofitting account structure onto one giant shared account later is painful.

resources.title: AWS — Organizing your AWS environment using multiple accounts

cards.prompt: On-demand vs reserved/savings plans vs spot instances
cards.answer: On-demand is pay-as-you-go with no commitment; reservations and savings plans trade a one- or three-year commitment for large discounts; spot instances use spare capacity at the deepest discounts but can be reclaimed at short notice.

right.title: Spot
points: Diversify instance types to reduce interruptions

cards.explanation: Cover the steady baseline with commitments, burst with on-demand, and run interruption-tolerant work — batch jobs, CI runners, stateless workers behind a queue — on spot. Anything on spot must checkpoint or be safely retryable.

cards.prompt: Disaster-recovery strategies: backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active
cards.answer: In increasing cost and decreasing recovery time: restore from backups into a new region (hours); pilot light (data replicated, core minimal, scale up on failover — tens of minutes); warm standby (a scaled-down full copy running — minutes); active-active (serving from several regions — near zero).

left.title: Backup & restore / pilot light
points: Restore data and infrastructure from code
Pilot light: replicated data, minimal core
Scale up only when disaster strikes

cards.explanation: Choose from business RPO (how much data you may lose) and RTO (how long you may be down), not from ambition. The failure mode common to all of them is an untested failover: run game days, because the recovery path is exercised far less often than the normal one.

resources.title: AWS — Disaster recovery options in the cloud

cards.prompt: Leadership worries about vendor lock-in. How do you reason about it rather than avoiding managed services altogether?
cards.answer: Treat lock-in as a cost to weigh, not a thing to avoid: managed services buy speed and reliability now; portability has a price paid every day (lowest-common-denominator designs, running more yourself). Keep portability where it is cheap — containers, open protocols (Postgres, S3-compatible APIs, OpenTelemetry), infrastructure as code — and accept deep integration where it pays.
cards.explanation: Multi-cloud "just in case" usually doubles operational cost for a migration that never happens. Isolate provider-specific code behind small adapters where the switch risk is real, and keep your data exportable — data gravity is the real lock-in.

resources.title: Martin Fowler — Don't get locked up into avoiding lock-in
